# Draft:Perm Cultural Revolution

----
The Perm Cultural Revolution was a cultural policy initiative implemented in the city of Perm and the Perm Krai region of Russia from 2008 to the early 2010s. The project sought to transform Perm from a predominantly industrial city into a cultural center through contemporary art, festivals, and urban cultural programs.
Background
In the late 2000s, Perm’s regional authorities began supporting cultural initiatives as part of a broader strategy to rebrand the city and stimulate social and economic development. The approach emphasized contemporary art, public exhibitions, and international cultural exchange, marking a departure from traditional state-centered cultural institutions.
The initiative gained momentum in 2008 with a series of high-profile contemporary art events and exhibitions that positioned culture as a central element of urban policy rather than a peripheral activity.
Major initiatives
Key components of the Perm Cultural Revolution included contemporary art exhibitions, festivals, and the establishment of new cultural institutions. These initiatives aimed to integrate art into public spaces and attract both local audiences and international attention.
According to academic research, the project represented an attempt to apply culture as an instrument of urban transformation, comparable to similar strategies used in European post-industrial cities, though adapted to the Russian political and cultural context.
International coverage
In 2009, The New York Times described efforts to reinvent Perm as a cultural center, portraying the initiative as an attempt to initiate a “cultural revolution” in an industrial Russian city.
In 2011, a follow-up feature in The New York Times referred to Perm as an “emerging cultural hotspot”, highlighting its contemporary art scene and growing international visibility.
The project was also analyzed by international cultural platforms such as Transit Online, which examined the Perm Cultural Revolution as a case of culture-driven urban transformation supported by regional political leadership.
European media also covered Perm’s cultural transformation. The Swiss newspaper Neue Zürcher Zeitung reported on Perm’s cultural policy experiments, placing them in the broader context of culture-led urban development in Russia.
The cultural transformation of Perm also attracted attention in francophone academic discourse, where the city was described as a laboratory of a “cultural revolution”, with analyses focusing on public art projects and debates surrounding contemporary art in the urban space.
Major French media also reported on Perm’s cultural transformation. The newspaper Le Monde covered the city’s cultural initiatives and conflicts surrounding contemporary art projects, framing them as part of an unfinished cultural revolution.
Other English-language media also linked Perm’s cultural initiatives to governor Oleg Chirkunov. Reporting highlighted the region’s efforts to shift from an industrial identity toward culture-driven development, including major festivals and institutional reforms that became associated with what was described as a “Perm cultural revolution.”
The project also attracted attention from international business media. The Financial Times examined Perm’s cultural strategy as an attempt to use culture-led development to counter population decline and economic stagnation in a post-industrial Russian city.
Reception and criticism
While the Perm Cultural Revolution was praised by some observers for its ambition and international visibility, it also faced criticism. Academic analyses note tensions between imported contemporary art models and local cultural traditions, as well as debates over public spending priorities.
Aftermath
By the early 2010s, changes in regional political leadership led to a decline in official support for the project. Several initiatives were discontinued or restructured, and the period commonly referred to as the Perm Cultural Revolution came to an end. Nevertheless, the project remains a notable example in discussions of cultural policy and urban transformation in contemporary Russia.
